hmmt-nov-2011-guts-01.title: Compute the sum modulo 2012
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-01.body:
$1+2+\cdots+2014=\frac{2014\cdot2015}{2}=1007\cdot2015$. Since $2015\equiv3\pmod{2012}$, this is $\equiv3021\equiv1009\pmod{2012}$.

(Do not halve after reducing: $2$ is not invertible mod $2012$.)

**Answer: 1009**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-01.title: Cancel a full block
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-01.body:
The first $2012$ terms sum to $\frac{2012\cdot2013}{2}=1006\cdot2013\equiv1006\pmod{2012}$ (because $2013\equiv1$). The remaining terms $2013+2014\equiv1+2=3$. Total $\equiv1009$.

**Answer: 1009**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-02.title: Coordinates
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-02.body:
Put $B=(0,0)$, $C=(4,0)$, $A=(0,6)$, $D=(4,6)$, $E=(3,0)$. $F$ is halfway between $AB$ ($x=0$) and $CD$ ($x=4$), so $F$ has $x=2$ on line $AE$: $y=6-2x=2$, $F=(2,2)$. Line $DF$ has slope $\frac{6-2}{4-2}=2$ and meets $y=0$ at $x=2-1=1$. So $G=(1,0)$ and $BG=1$.

**Answer: 1**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-04.title: Compare pairs
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-04.body:
$54\sqrt3<108$ since $\sqrt3<2$, while $144>108$, so $54\sqrt3<144$.

To compare $54\sqrt3$ with $108(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)$, divide by $54$: compare $\sqrt3$ with $2(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)$. Squaring the positive quantity $2(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)$ gives $4(8-4\sqrt3)=32-16\sqrt3$; we want $3<32-16\sqrt3$, i.e. $16\sqrt3<29$, i.e. $\sqrt3<\frac{29}{16}$, true because $\frac{841}{256}>3$. So $\sqrt3<2(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)$ and $54\sqrt3$ is smallest ($\approx93.5$, versus $\approx111.8$ and $144$).

**Answer: $54\sqrt3$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-05.title: Each fold removes one side length from the perimeter
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-05.body:
Folding a rectangle in half along a line parallel to one pair of edges halves the other pair, so the perimeter $2a+2b$ drops by the length of the side that is halved. The original perimeter is $2\cdot\frac{17}2+2\cdot11=39$.

We want the largest total drop over two folds. Halving $11$ twice drops $11+\frac{11}2=16.5$; halving $\frac{17}2$ twice drops $\frac{17}2+\frac{17}4=12.75$; halving each side once (in either order) drops $11+\frac{17}2=19.5$. The best is $19.5$, giving perimeter $39-\frac{39}2=\frac{39}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{39}{2}$ inches**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-06.title: Count outfits
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-06.body:
Outfits with $3$ shirts: $4\cdot3\cdot2=24$ ordered choices. Outfits with $4$ shirts: $4!=24$. Total $48$ outfits (equivalently: choose the innermost three shirts in order, $4\cdot3\cdot2$, then either add the last shirt or not).

Each outfit lasts $3$ days: $48\cdot3=144$.

**Answer: 144 days**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-07.title: Prime by prime
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-07.body:
$54000=2^4\cdot3^3\cdot5^3$. Write each of $a,b,c$ in prime factors; for each prime we need $4a_i+2b_i+c_i$ to equal the exponent.
- Prime $2$ (exponent $4$): $(a,b,c)$ exponents $(1,0,0),(0,2,0),(0,1,2),(0,0,4)$: $4$ ways.
- Primes $3$ and $5$ (exponent $3$): $(0,1,1),(0,0,3)$: $2$ ways each. (Note $a$-exponent must be $0$ since $4>3$.)

Total $4\cdot2\cdot2=16$.

**Answer: 16**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-08.title: Rewrite the fraction
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-08.body:
Write $\frac{ab+c}{a+b+c}=1+\frac{ab-a-b}{a+b+c}$. The numerator $ab-a-b=(a-1)(b-1)-1$ is negative only when $(a-1)(b-1)<1$, i.e. $a=1$ or $b=1$. Otherwise the fraction is at least $1$.

Say $a=1$: the value is $1-\frac{1}{b+c+1}$, which is smallest when $b+c$ is smallest: $b=c=1$, giving $1-\frac13=\frac23$.

**Answer: $\frac23$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-09.title: Tangent sides
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-09.body:
Let $O$ be the centre. $\angle WYZ=60^\circ=\angle YXZ$, so $YW$ is tangent to $\Omega$ at $Y$ (tangent-chord angle); similarly $ZW$ is tangent at $Z$. The part of triangle $WYZ$ outside $\Omega$ is the triangle $WYZ$ minus the circular segment cut by chord $YZ$ (which has central angle $120^\circ$).

The segment area is $\frac13\pi-[OYZ]$. With $YZ=\sqrt3$ and $WY=WZ=\sqrt3$: $[WYZ]=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}$, and $[OYZ]=\frac12\sin120^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}$.

Required area $=[WYZ]-\bigl(\frac\pi3-[OYZ]\bigr)=\frac{3\sqrt3}4-\frac\pi3+\frac{\sqrt3}4=\sqrt3-\frac\pi3=\frac{3\sqrt3-\pi}{3}$.

**Answer: $\frac{3\sqrt3-\pi}{3}$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-10.title: Bound D from both sides
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-10.body:
We need $-1<a^2-Db^2<1$ for all such $a,b$, i.e. $\frac{a^2-1}{b^2}<D<\frac{a^2+1}{b^2}$ (for $b\ne0$; $b=0$ is automatic as $a^2<1$).

The lower bound $\frac{a^2-1}{b^2}$ is largest when $a$ is as large as possible and $b$ as large as possible: it approaches $\frac{1/16-1}{1/16}=-15$ but never reaches it since $|a|,|b|<\frac14$ strictly. The upper bound $\frac{a^2+1}{b^2}$ is smallest approaching $\frac{0+1}{1/16}=16$ (not reached). So $D$ must satisfy $-15\le D\le16$ (the endpoints are allowed because the inequalities are strict only for values of $a,b$ not attaining the extreme).

Count: $16-(-15)+1=32$.

**Answer: 32**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-11.title: Group by gcd value
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-11.body:
$91=7\cdot13$, so $\gcd(n,91)\in\{1,7,13,91\}$. For $1\le n\le91$: $\gcd=91$ only for $n=91$ ($1$ value); $\gcd=7$ for multiples of $7$ other than $91$ ($13-1=12$ values); $\gcd=13$ for multiples of $13$ other than $91$ ($7-1=6$ values); $\gcd=1$ for the remaining $91-1-12-6=72$.

Sum $=91+12\cdot7+6\cdot13+72=91+84+78+72=325$.

**Answer: 325**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-12.title: Count with the three constraints
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-12.body:
The conditions are: $p_4>p_1$, $p_5>p_2$, $p_5>p_1$ (writing $p_i$ for the difficulty of problem $i$). Among the $120$ orderings of difficulties, half satisfy $p_4>p_1$ and, independently, half satisfy $p_5>p_2$: $120\cdot\frac14=30$.

Among those $30$, the bad ones violate $p_5>p_1$ as well, which (with $p_4>p_1$ and $p_5>p_2$) forces the single relative order $p_4>p_1>p_5>p_2$ of the four problems $1,2,4,5$. Of the $\binom42\cdot\binom22=6$ relative orders of these four satisfying $p_4>p_1$ and $p_5>p_2$, exactly $1$ is bad, so $\frac56\cdot30=25$ orderings are good.

**Answer: 25**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-13.title: Independent legs
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-13.body:
Each leg ends up with one sock, one shoe, and one snow-shoe, put on in a random order. The chance that a given leg has them in the order sock, shoe, snow-shoe is $\frac1{3!}=\frac16$. The four legs are independent, so the probability is $\left(\frac16\right)^4=\frac1{1296}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{1296}$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-14.title: Right angles at $M$ and $L$
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-14.body:
Let $E$ be the midpoint of $AO$ and $D$ the midpoint of $AM$. $E$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AM$, so $ED\perp AM$, and with $D$ and $E$ midpoints of $AM$ and $AO$, $DE\parallel MO$; hence $MO\perp AM$, i.e. $\angle M=90^\circ$. Similarly $\angle L=90^\circ$.

Then $AO^2=AM^2+MO^2=100+121=221$ and $AL=\sqrt{AO^2-OL^2}=\sqrt{221-144}=\sqrt{77}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{77}$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-15.title: Which numbers have a given $L$
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-15.body:
If $L(a)=x$, then $a=px$ where $p$ is a prime not exceeding the smallest prime factor of $x$ (otherwise a larger proper divisor appears). So:
- For $x=2,4,8,10,16,20,40$ (smallest prime factor $2$): only $a=2x$, one value each.
- For $x=5$ (smallest prime factor $5$): $a=2\cdot5,3\cdot5,5\cdot5$, three values.

$m,n$ composite means $L(m),L(n)>1$. The factorizations $80=L(m)L(n)$ with both factors from the list: $\{2,40\},\{4,20\},\{5,16\},\{8,10\}$, each in two orders. Counting choices: $(1\cdot1)+(1\cdot1)+(3\cdot1)+(1\cdot1)=6$ for one order, doubled for ordered pairs: $12$.

**Answer: 12**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-16.title: Backtrack one move from the sorted order
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-16.body:
Start from the sorted order and undo one move: pick one of the $17$ cards and move it to one of the $16$ other places: $17\cdot16=272$ resulting orders (each is unsorted). But some orders arise twice: moving card $k$ between $k+1$ and $k+2$ gives the same order as moving card $k+1$ between $k-1$ and $k$ (both swap adjacent cards $k$ and $k+1$). These are exactly the $16$ adjacent swaps, each counted twice and nothing else coincides.

So the number of distinct orders is $17\cdot16-16=256$.

**Answer: 256**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-17.title: Product of divisors
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-17.body:
$p(n)=n^{d(n)/2}$, where $d(n)$ is the number of divisors (pair each divisor $f$ with $n/f$). It is a perfect square iff $n$ is a perfect square or $4\mid d(n)$.

$2310=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11$ is squarefree, so its $32$ divisors are products of $k$ distinct primes, with $d=2^k$. For $k\ge2$, $4\mid2^k$: $p(n)$ is a square. For $k=0$, $n=1$: $p(1)=1$ is a square (and $1$ is a perfect square). For $k=1$, $n$ prime, $p(n)=n$ is not a square.

So the answer is $32-5=27$.

**Answer: 27**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-18.title: Area as a fraction of rectangle $ACGE$
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-18.body:
$AG=1$ means the edge length is $s=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, and $AC=s\sqrt2=\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}$. Triangle $AOP$ lies in the plane of rectangle $ACGE$. $OP$ is parallel to $CG$ with $OP=\frac s2=\frac1{2\sqrt3}$, and the distance from $A$ to line $OP$ is $\frac12AC=\frac{\sqrt2}{2\sqrt3}$. So $[AOP]=\frac12\cdot\frac1{2\sqrt3}\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt2}{24}$ (which is $\frac18[ACGE]$).

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt2}{24}$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-19.title: Similar triangles
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-19.body:
Triangles $XYC$ and $ZWA$ are congruent (angle chasing around the rectangle, with $XY=ZW$), so $YC=AW=1$. Also $\triangle XYC\sim\triangle WXB$, giving $\frac{BX}{BW}=\frac{CY}{CX}$, i.e. $\frac{BX}{2}=\frac{1}{7-BX}$ (as $BW=2$, $CX=7-BX$).

Thus $BX(7-BX)=2$, i.e. $BX^2-7BX+2=0$, so $BX=\frac{7\pm\sqrt{41}}2$. Since $BX<XC$, $BX=\frac{7-\sqrt{41}}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{7-\sqrt{41}}{2}$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-20.title: Complement: all three Spanish teams in the same half
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-20.body:
The final has fewer than $2$ Spanish teams only if all three Spanish teams were in the same half of the bracket (then two of them meet before the final and only one survives). Random pairings every round are equivalent to splitting the $16$ teams into two groups of $8$ and taking a winner from each.

Fix the group of Spanish team $A$. The probability that $B$ is in the same group is $\frac7{15}$, and then $C$ also is with probability $\frac6{14}$. So the bad probability is $\frac7{15}\cdot\frac6{14}=\frac15$ and the answer is $1-\frac15=\frac45$.

**Answer: $\frac45$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-22.title: Equal tangents
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-22.body:
The two incircles are tangent to each other exactly when they touch $BD$ at the same point. The incircle of $ABD$ touches $BD$ at distance $\frac{BA+BD-AD}{2}$ from $B$; the incircle of $CBD$ touches it at distance $\frac{BC+BD-CD}{2}$. Setting equal: $23-AD=24-CD$, i.e. $CD-AD=1$.

With $CD+AD=27$ we get $CD=14$, $AD=13$, so $\frac{CD}{DA}=\frac{14}{13}$.

**Answer: $\frac{14}{13}$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-23.title: Split 792 into 8, 9, 11
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-23.body:
$792=8\cdot9\cdot11$.
- $8\mid N$: $8\mid\overline{7C2}=702+10C$, so $8\mid 10C+6$, giving $C\in\{1,5,9\}$.
- $9\mid N$: $5+A+B+3+7+C+2=17+A+B+C\equiv0\pmod 9$ i.e. $A+B+C\in\{1,10,19\}$.
- $11\mid N$: alternating sum $5-A+B-3+7-C+2=11-A+B-C\equiv0$, so $B-A-C\in\{-11,0\}$.

Adding the last two conditions for $A+B+C$ and $B-A-C$ gives $2B$ even, so $B\in\{4,5\}$ (checking all combinations). Testing $C\in\{1,5,9\}$: the valid triples are $(0,5,5)$, $(4,5,1)$, $(6,4,9)$ (e.g. $5053752/792=6381$).

**Answer: $(0,5,5),(4,5,1),(6,4,9)$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-24.title: Split by the number of digits
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-24.body:
- $6$ digits: all three numbers have two digits: $90^3=729000$.
- $5$ digits: exactly one number is one-digit (the digit lengths are $1,2,2$ in some order). A $5$-digit $N$ is achievable iff its first digit is nonzero and the zeros can all be placed so that no number begins with $0$: with no zero digits $9^5=59049$; with one zero (positions $2$ to $5$) $4\cdot9^4=26244$; with two zeros (positions chosen among $2$ to $5$, not adjacent: $(2,4),(2,5),(3,5)$) $3\cdot9^3=2187$. Total $87480$.
- $4$ digits: lengths $1,1,2$ in some order. No zeros: $9^4=6561$; one zero (positions $2$ to $4$): $3\cdot9^3=2187$. Total $8748$.
- $3$ digits: all one-digit, no zeros: $9^3=729$.

Different digit-lengths give different $N$, and within each length the strings counted are exactly the achievable ones. Total $729000+87480+8748+729=825957$.

**Answer: 825957**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-26.title: Squaring
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-26.body:
Let $a=2+\frac25+4x$ and $b=\frac25-2+\frac25x$. Then $a+b=\frac{22}5x+\frac45$ is exactly the quantity under the right-hand root. So the equation is $\sqrt a+\sqrt b=\sqrt{a+b}$, and squaring gives $2\sqrt{ab}=0$: $a=0$ or $b=0$. Since $x>0$, $a>0$, so $b=0$: $\frac25x=\frac85$, $x=4$.

Check: $a=2.4+16=18.4$, $b=0$, right side $\sqrt{17.6+0.8}=\sqrt{18.4}$. 

**Answer: 4**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-27.title: Symmetry
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-27.body:
The first digit is $0$ or $1$ with equal probability, and the rule for later digits treats $0$ and $1$ symmetrically. So swapping all zeros and ones maps each outcome to an equally likely one; hence the expected number of zeros equals the expected number of ones, each $\frac42=2$.

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-29.title: Similar triangles and power of a point
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-29.body:
Let $E$ be the second intersection of $AM$ with the circumcircle. From $\angle BAD=\angle CAM$ we get $\triangle ADC\sim\triangle ABM$, so $AD=\frac{AC\cdot AB}{AM}=\frac{20}{AM}$.

By the law of cosines $\cos B=\frac{16+64-25}{2\cdot4\cdot8}=\frac{55}{64}$, so $AM^2=16+16-32\cdot\frac{55}{64}=\frac92$, $AM=\frac{3}{\sqrt2}=\frac{3\sqrt2}2$ and $AD=\frac{20\sqrt2}{3}$.

Power of the point $M$: $AM\cdot ME=BM\cdot MC=16$, so $ME=\frac{16\sqrt2}{3}$ and $AE=\frac{3\sqrt2}2+\frac{16\sqrt2}3=\frac{41\sqrt2}{6}$. Triangles $ABX$ and $AEC$ are similar, giving $AX=\frac{AB\cdot AC}{AE}=\frac{20}{AE}=\frac{120}{41\sqrt2}=\frac{60\sqrt2}{41}$.

Therefore $\frac{AX}{AD}=\frac{60\sqrt2/41}{20\sqrt2/3}=\frac{9}{41}$.

**Answer: $\frac9{41}$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-30.title: Construction and bound
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-30.body:
**Construction.** Take $999981,999982,\dots,1000018$ ($38$ numbers). Their digit sums are $45,\dots,53$ (for $999981$ to $999989$), $45,\dots,54$ (for $999990$ to $999999$), $1,\dots,10$ (for $1000000$ to $1000009$), and $2,\dots,10$ (for $1000010$ to $1000018$). None is divisible by $11$.

**Bound.** Suppose $39$ consecutive integers worked. Then they contain three consecutive full decades $10b,\dots,10b+9$ for $b=a-1,a,a+1$. Let $10a$ have digit sum $N$; the numbers $10a+1,\dots,10a+9$ have digit sums $N+1,\dots,N+9$, so $N\equiv1\pmod{11}$ (to avoid multiples of 11 and also $N$ itself). If the tens digit of $10a$ is not $9$, then $10(a+1)+9$ has digit sum $N+10\equiv0$, a contradiction. If it is $9$, then $10(a-1)$ has digit sum $N-1\equiv0$, again a contradiction. So at most $38$.

**Answer: 38**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-31.title: Checkerboard split
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-31.body:
Label the cells in checkerboard fashion with $0$ and $1$. Every 'X' consists of five cells with the same label, so the cells labelled $0$ and the cells labelled $1$ are colored independently, each in the same number of ways (the two classes are mirror images). Hence $N=a^2$ and $\sqrt N=a$, the number of ways to color the $0$-cells.

Let $a_{2n}$ be the number of colorings of the $0$-cells in a $3\times2n$ board, and $b_{2n}$ the number of such colorings in which the two $0$-cells of the last column are not both black (by symmetry this equals the number in which they are not both white). Looking at the last three $0$-cells (two in one column and one in the adjacent column, which can form part of an X only together with the earlier columns): either they all have the same color (2 ways for $a$, 1 way for $b$, and the rest is a $b_{2n-2}$ board), or not (6 ways for $a$, 5 for $b$, rest an $a_{2n-2}$ board). So $a_{2n}=6a_{2n-2}+2b_{2n-2}$ and $b_{2n}=5a_{2n-2}+b_{2n-2}$. Eliminating $b$ gives $a_{2n+2}=7a_{2n}+4a_{2n-2}$ with $a_0=1$, $a_2=8$.

Then $a_4=60$, $a_6=452$, $a_8=3404$, $a_{10}=25636$. (A direct computer count of both color classes also gives $25636$ each.)

**Answer: 25636**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-32.title: Inverse functions
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-32.body:
Note that $\left(x^3+\frac38\right)^3=x^9+\frac98x^6+\frac{27}{64}x^3+\frac{27}{512}$, and $\frac{219}{512}-\frac{27}{512}=\frac{192}{512}=\frac38$. So the equation is $\left(x^3+\frac38\right)^3=x-\frac38$, i.e. $x^3+\frac38=\sqrt[3]{x-\frac38}$.

The functions $g(x)=x^3+\frac38$ and $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x-\frac38}$ are increasing inverses of each other, and the equation says $g(x)=f(x)$. For increasing inverse functions, $f(x)=g(x)$ forces $f(x)=x$: if $f(x)=y\neq x$ then $g(x)=y$ means $f(y)=x$, and monotonicity gives a contradiction ($x<y\Rightarrow f(x)<f(y)$, i.e. $y<x$). So we need $x^3+\frac38=x$, i.e. $x^3-x+\frac38=0$, which factors as $\left(x-\frac12\right)\left(x^2+\frac12x-\frac34\right)=0$.

The roots are $x=\frac12$ and $x=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{13}}{4}$.

**Answer: $\frac12,\ \frac{-1\pm\sqrt{13}}{4}$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-33.title: Homothety at A
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-33.body:
The homothety centred at $A$ taking $\Gamma$ to the circumcircle sends $D\to B$, $E\to C$, so $DE\parallel BC$ and $\frac{DE}{BC}=\frac{AP}{AO}$ where $P,O$ are the centres of $\Gamma$ and the circumcircle. The tangency point $X$ of $\Gamma$ with $BC$ goes to the point $Y$ on the circumcircle where the tangent is parallel to $BC$, i.e. the midpoint of arc $BC$; so $AX$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

Let $Z$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$ and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Then $\frac{AP}{AO}=\frac{ZX}{ZM}$. Using $a=8,b=7,c=5$: $BZ=\frac{c^2+a^2-b^2}{2a}=\frac52$, $BX=\frac{ac}{b+c}=\frac{10}3$, $BM=4$. So $ZX=\frac{10}3-\frac52=\frac56$ and $ZM=4-\frac52=\frac32$.

$DE=8\cdot\frac{5/6}{3/2}=\frac{40}9$.

**Answer: $\frac{40}{9}$**

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-34.title: Estimate with the prime number theorem
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-34.body:
This is an estimation problem. The official answer is $\mathbf{365851}$ digits (the number $843301\#-1$ was then the largest known prime of the form $p\#-1$).

A good estimate: $\ln(p\#)=\theta(p)\approx p$, so $p\#\approx e^{843301}$, which has about $\frac{843301}{\ln 10}\approx366{,}240$ digits, within $0.2\%$ of the true value $365851$.

**Scoring:** $\max\{\lfloor60(\frac13-|\ln(A/d)|)\rfloor,0\}$, so you need to be within about $39\%$ for any credit.

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-35.title: Official data
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-35.body:
This is an estimation (research) question with no derivation. The official figures: Google reported $G=7350$ hits and Bing $B=6080$, so $\frac BG=\frac{6080}{7350}\approx0.82721$.

**Scoring:** $\max(0,\lfloor20(1-20|a-k|/k)\rfloor)$ where $k=0.82721$ and $a$ is your answer: you must be within $5\%$ of the true value for any credit.

hmmt-nov-2011-guts-36.title: Dates
hmmt-nov-2011-guts-36.body:
I: Hilbert Problems, 1900. A: Zermelo's axioms, 1908. J: Incompleteness Theorems, 1931. C: Collatz Conjecture, 1937. B: Category Theory, 1942-45. M: Nash Equilibrium, 1950. H: Chomsky hierarchy, 1956. O: Quicksort, 1960. D: Erdos number defined, 1969. E: first US IMO delegation, 1974. F: Four Color Theorem, 1976. L: Diaconis shuffles, 1992. N: Wiles's proof of FLT, 1995 (completed 1994-95). G: HMMT founded, 1998. K: Clay Millennium prize, 2000.

So the full order is **IAJCBMHODEFLNGK**.

**Scoring:** a subset of $n\ge6$ events in the correct relative order scores $2(n-5)$; any error scores $0$.
